An alternating quantity varying sinusoidally with time can be represented by a phasor using Euler's formula and rotating vectors. 

Let an alternating voltage be $v(t) = V_m \sin(\omega t + \phi)$.
According to Euler's identity, the complex exponential form is:
$$v(t) = \text{Im}\left( V_m e^{j(\omega t + \phi)} \right) = \text{Im}\left( (V_m e^{j\phi}) e^{j\omega t} \right)$$

Here, the term $\mathbf{V} = V_m \angle \phi$ (or in RMS, $\frac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}} \angle \phi$) is a complex number independent of time, called a **phasor**. It represents the magnitude and initial phase angle of the alternating quantity as a stationary vector rotating counter-clockwise at a constant angular velocity $\omega$.
proTip: Phasors simplify steady-state AC circuit analysis by converting differential equations into simple algebraic complex number equations.
